title: Communication and Collaboration in SRE
subtitle: Turn shared operational knowledge into coordinated engineering
summary: Pip’s production meeting has become a list of busy people. The crew returns it to service behavior: changes, incidents, trends, and assigned improvements. Shared agendas and clear ownership help development partners and remote colleagues contribute.

concepts.title: Production meetings as a feedback mechanism
concepts.body: Pip replaces status-by-person with a review of the harbor service. Changes, trends, incidents, and paging connect observed behavior to architecture and implementation. A growing query delay leads to a jointly owned investigation with developers. Pip revisits earlier actions so the meeting closes the production feedback loop.

concepts.title: Shared agendas and inclusive participation
concepts.body: Pip’s remote colleague cannot get a word into the crowded room. A shared agenda prepared beforehand collects evidence, questions, and links. The chair makes participation deliberate and records decisions and actions. Pip welcomes representatives or written input when relevant partners cannot all attend.

concepts.title: Cross-site ownership and common direction
concepts.body: Pip merges complementary dashboard work from two sites. Distributed expertise brings communication delays and incomplete local context. A common vision, recorded decisions, owned components, and continuing maintenance commitments reduce those costs. The chapter’s Viceroy experience reminds Pip that a useful patch can still leave remote owners and features unsupported.

concepts.title: Early collaboration with product engineering
concepts.body: Pip defines interfaces with product engineers before the migration hardens. Product brings business behavior; SRE brings infrastructure, failure, and scale experience. The chapter’s DFP migration compared old and new generated outputs while infrastructure and business logic changed. Pip resolves discrepancies before traffic moves, allowing operational preparation and implementation to proceed together.

misconceptions.claim: A production meeting is mainly a round of individual progress reports.
misconceptions.correction: Its central purpose is a shared view of service behavior and concrete improvements informed by operations.

misconceptions.claim: A merged codebase automatically gives a cross-site project clear ownership.
misconceptions.correction: Maintainers, decision practices, and long-term contribution commitments still need explicit agreement.

scenario.title: Resolve a production disagreement
scenario.context: A product team wants a launch tomorrow; SRE sees an untested dependency path. Both teams have partial evidence and a shared customer deadline.

options.label: Write the disagreement and testable decision in a shared review
options.benefit: A common record lets both teams inspect assumptions and agree on evidence.
options.cost: The written review may delay launch while evidence is gathered.
options.consequence: A load test and rollback owner make the launch decision explicit.

options.label: Resolve it in a private escalation
options.benefit: A private decision is faster and limits meeting time.
options.cost: Context is lost and the same disagreement can return.
options.consequence: The escalation approves launch without resolving the dependency risk.

scenario.debrief: A shared review lets product and SRE combine their different evidence and assign the missing validation. Record interfaces, decisions, and owners so remote teammates and future work can use the result.

quiz.question: Which question belongs in a production meeting’s paging review?
options: Which individual completed the largest number of operational tasks?
Should this event have paged, and was the response appropriate?
Did every configured alert fire at least once this week?
quiz.explanation: Paging review checks alert value and operational response, not individual productivity.

quiz.question: What made the DFP migration’s output comparison valuable?
options: It allowed infrastructure behavior to substitute for business-logic validation
It demonstrated that both databases used the same internal schema
It exposed behavioral discrepancies before the replacement served users
quiz.explanation: Matching old and new generated outputs supported a seamless migration.

quiz.question: What protects a cross-site project from abandoned contributed features?
options: Explicit ownership and a commitment to maintain and integrate contributions
Accepting every patch without shared direction
Restricting decisions to unrecorded local conversations
quiz.explanation: Sustained ownership matters after an initial contributor returns to other work.

exercise.title: Build a shared production decision
exercise.prompt: Prepare an agenda item about a risky dependency change that needs input from product and SRE.
